title: Why Slurry Handling Is Becoming More Than a Pump Problem
excerpt: Mining isn’t a clean process, and it doesn’t stop once material has been taken out of the ground.
html:
Mining isn’t a clean process, and it doesn’t stop once material has been taken out of the ground.

The ore still needs to be processed, separated and moved through different stages before the valuable material can be recovered.

As the ore is processed, it is crushed and mixed with water, creating a slurry that can be transported through the plant.

This is the point where the process becomes significantly more challenging.

Unlike clean liquids, slurry carries solid materials, making the mixture heavier and more abrasive. If conditions are not carefully controlled, material can settle, and in some cases, the slurry becomes thick and corrosive. This places much greater demands on the equipment used to transport it.

On paper, slurry handling is simple: move material from one stage to the next.

In practice, reliably doing that is where the trouble begins.

What changes from one slurry application to another

Slurries vary.

There’s no universal answer to how easy they’ll be to move.

Meaning there’s no uniform way to do so.

One application might involve a relatively thin mixture with fine particles, while another could require handling larger, abrasive solids. Both are considered slurries, yet each places very different demands on the equipment used.

Solids concentration is another key factor. As that proportion rises, the slurry becomes denser and more difficult to transport. Particle size, viscosity, and abrasiveness also contribute.

Then there’s what needs to be achieved.

The required flow, the distance involved, and the pressure needed all play a role.

What works perfectly in one operation might be hopeless in another.

Where does the pump fit into the wider system?

The pump is fundamental to moving slurry, but it does not operate in isolation.

The slurry must still travel through pipework, bends, valves, and hoses before reaching the next stage. The size and layout of the system directly affect how easily the material moves.

This means choosing a suitable pump is only part of the job. If the surrounding system makes it harder for the slurry to travel as intended, the pump alone cannot solve the problem.

The pump needs to suit both the material being moved and the system it is moving through.

Why suppliers are expanding what they can provide

The challenges involved in slurry handling help explain why some suppliers are broadening what they can offer.

A good example of this is Metso agreeing to take over Valmet's pump business. The deal is set to add two additional pump technologies to Metso's current range, giving it more options for difficult materials like thick, abrasive, or high-solids slurries.

Metso currently provides several components for slurry-handling systems, such as pumps, valves, and hoses. This acquisition goes beyond simply adding products to its range because it allows the company to handle a wider variety of applications and offer a broader range of solutions.

The more the offering expands, the more the people selling it need to understand both the product and its application

What does this mean for technical sales?

As solutions become broader, the technical side does too.

Knowing the product range still matters, but it’s only part of the job. Before recommending anything, the salesperson needs to know what the customer is trying to achieve, what’s already in place and where the real problem is.

That means asking the right questions, not just matching a requirement to a model number.

They need enough technical understanding to spot where the pump fits, when the problem goes beyond it, and when to bring in applications or engineering support.

In the end, the customer isn’t buying a pump just to have one. They want to move difficult material, and they want it to work.

The more of that problem the supplier takes on, the more important it is for the person selling the solution to understand both the product and the job it’s meant to do.

title: Smarter Buildings, Greater Demands
excerpt: In 2025, the commercial building automation market was estimated at $21.23 billion. In 2026, this is predicted to rise by around 6%, with an early-year forecast anticipating $22.53 billion by year-end.
html:
In 2025, the commercial building automation market was estimated at $21.23 billion. In 2026, this is predicted to rise by around 6%, with an early-year forecast anticipating $22.53 billion by year-end.

(US Commercial Building Automation Market Size and Share 2031, 2026)

Building automation relies on a combination of technologies and continuous investment. Controls, sensors, and software work together to manage heating, cooling, and ventilation. Regardless of how advanced these systems become, skilled professionals are always needed to design, install, and maintain them.

As HVAC automation evolves, so do the technical demands on the businesses delivering it. Increased investment creates opportunity, but turning advanced technology into dependable systems requires the ability to address increasingly complex customer needs.

Investment Creates Opportunity

Investment is not confined to a single area of BAS. Funds may go toward new systems, upgrades, or the services required to keep them operating efficiently.

New construction remains one source of demand, since every new commercial building needs heating, cooling, and ventilation systems. Meanwhile, existing buildings offer opportunities for retrofits, upgrades, and preventive maintenance of aging equipment and controls. Installing and commissioning new HVAC systems can lead to long-term service agreements.

Smarter Systems Need Skilled People

When people think of automation, they often assume it eliminates the human element. In reality, modern systems still rely on physical equipment like controls and sensors, as well as software. While these machines may require less direct input, their operation is much more advanced and demands specialized knowledge.

As technology progresses and investment increases, the need intensifies for professionals who can handle complex tasks such as installation, testing, troubleshooting, and maintenance. The market’s growth depends not only on adopting new technology, but also on having enough skilled people to support it.

Employment of US HVAC technicians is projected to grow by 8% between 2024 and 2034, notably outpacing the estimated 3% growth across all occupations. On average, around 40,100 openings are expected each year, with many resulting from retirements and career changes.

These figures highlight the scale of workforce demand facing the industry. Meeting that demand will be important if businesses are to install, maintain, and support increasingly advanced building-automation systems.

(Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers, 2024)

Installation is only the beginning. Each new system adds to the growing number of systems already operating in commercial buildings, all requiring ongoing support.

As the installed base grows, so does the volume of equipment requiring support. Companies must have enough skilled professionals to manage both new installations and existing systems.

This creates demand beyond the initial project. Maintenance agreements and technical support can provide recurring work, while upgrades and repairs extend the customer relationship over time.

What Growth Will Depend On

The commercial building automation market is expected to continue growing, creating opportunities across new installations, system upgrades, controls, servicing, and long-term technical support.

However, smarter technology cannot operate on its own. Every successful project still relies on people who understand customer needs, recommend the right solutions, and support systems throughout their lifecycle.

For HVAC businesses, turning market growth into lasting value depends on having the expertise to deliver reliable systems and build long-term customer relationships beyond initial installation.

title: Can the Pump Industry Keep Up With Rising US Water Investment?
excerpt: In the first five months of 2026, US state and local construction spending within several areas of water infrastructure increased. The data shows:
html:
In the first five months of 2026, US state and local construction spending within several areas of water infrastructure increased. The data shows:

$6.927 billion on sewage lines and pump stations, up 3.1%

$8.399 billion on wastewater-treatment plants, up 5.7% $4.013 billion on water-treatment plants, up 7.7% year on year

(U.S. Census Bureau, Construction Spending, July 1, 2026)

The increase isn’t meaningless. It shows a commitment to maintaining, expanding, and modernizing essential water infrastructure. This is most evident in how water treatment plants saw the fastest growth.

These projects show the need for clean water supply, wastewater treatment, and reliable sewage infrastructure. However, none of this infrastructure can operate without pumps and fluid-handling equipment.

Pumps already sit at the epicenter of the water industry, and where spending increases, so does opportunity. However, opportunity doesn’t come without pressure. Companies need the expertise to specify, sell, install, commission, and maintain.

What Increased Spending Means for the Pump Market

For pump suppliers, this growth could lead to more inquiries, more contracts, new partnerships, and much greater demand for technical support. Supplying the equipment is one part of the opportunity.

Every project has different requirements. It’s not the one-size-fits-all solution it may appear to be on the surface. The right pump is determined by factors like what it needs to move, where it operates, and how the wider system works.

Customers may therefore need help choosing the right equipment, as well as support throughout its life cycle.

Increased spending generates more work across the market and substantially raises demands on engineers, suppliers, and service technicians. While this expansion offers opportunities for development and innovation, only those prepared to address the resulting operational, technical, and personnel challenges will fully benefit.

Where the Pressure Could Fall

Growth affects different roles at different stages. Mechanical engineers help assess applications and select equipment. Sales engineers help turn technical needs into workable solutions. Field service technicians install, commission, and support the equipment.

Regardless of the role, the impact remains the same: the more projects, the more pressure across the whole chain. However, it is likely that field service technicians feel it the most.

With each new project, technicians could face higher workloads, tighter deadlines, and more challenging technical tasks.

Every new installation adds to the already growing number of pumps operating in the field. The more equipment, the more servicing, repairs, and replacement work needed over time. Unlike project sales, field service demand continues after construction ends.

Opportunity Depends on Expertise

The impact of this investment goes beyond the initial projects. More work means more equipment to specify, install, and maintain, creating continued demand throughout the pump industry.

However, the opportunity relies on having the technical capacity to support it. Pump companies need the right people across the board to meet growing demand and support the equipment already operating in the field.

Investment creates opportunity, but turning it into long-term growth requires expertise.
